# Workflow dependency lockfiles
A lockfile pins every action your workflows depend on to a verified commit, so the code you reviewed is the code that runs.
## Why lock workflow dependencies?
Workflows often reference an action by a tag or branch, such as `uses: octo-org/deploy-action@v3` or `uses: octo-org/deploy-action@main`. GitHub Actions resolves that reference to whatever commit the tag or branch points to at run time.
Tags and branches can move. As a result, the code that runs is not guaranteed to be the code that the workflow author originally reviewed. If an upstream maintainer's account is compromised and a tag is repointed, your repositories could run malicious code.
A workflow dependency lockfile pins a commit SHA to every action your workflows depend on, including transitive dependencies. It doesn't pin calls to reusable workflows (`jobs.<job_id>.uses`). To pin a reusable workflow, reference it by its full commit SHA. A lockfile controls which action code runs on the runner. It doesn't control other build inputs, such as input parameters, secrets, or the runner image. A lockfile gives you the following for the action code it covers:
* Reproducible resolution of action dependencies
* Reviewable dependency changes and Dependabot version updates
* An auditable inventory of your CI/CD systems' action dependencies
## How does the lockfile work?
The lockfile is defined in a repository at `.github/workflows/actions.lock`. It's generated by `gh actions-lock`, a GitHub CLI extension, and should never be edited by hand.
You can onboard a repository's workflows to the lockfile one at a time or all at once. After a workflow is onboarded:
* Every action dependency the workflow uses must be present in the lockfile.
* The locked commit is what runs when the workflow executes, and what allowed actions policies check.
* This commit must be reachable from the branch or tag recorded for it in the lockfile, in the action's own repository. A commit that exists only in a fork, or that's no longer reachable from that branch or tag, is rejected when the workflow runs.
A lockfile covers the workflows in its own repository, including transitive dependencies (actions that *your action dependencies* use), **except** for dependencies of reusable workflow calls. Reusable workflows can have their own lockfiles too. A reusable workflow's dependencies are covered by the lockfile of the repository where it's defined, not by the lockfile of the repository that calls it.
## What does the lockfile record?
The lockfile has two sections. `workflows` records which dependencies each onboarded workflow uses, and `dependencies` records which commit each of those references resolves to.

# Docs: https://gh.io/actions-lockfile

# Reviewing deployments
You can approve or reject jobs awaiting review.
## Approving or rejecting a job
1. Navigate to the workflow run that requires review. For more information about navigating to a workflow run, see [Viewing workflow run history](/en/actions/how-tos/monitor-workflows/view-workflow-run-history).
2. If the run requires review, you will see a notification for the review request. On the notification, click **Review deployments**.
3. Select the job environment(s) to approve or reject. Optionally, leave a comment.
4. Approve or reject:
   * To approve the job, click **Approve and deploy**. Once a job is approved (and any other deployment protection rules have passed), the job will proceed. At this point, the job can access any secrets stored in the environment.
   * To reject the job, click **Reject**. If a job is rejected, the workflow will fail.
> [!NOTE]
> If the targeted environment is configured to prevent self-approvals for deployments, you will not be able to approve a deployment from a workflow run you initiated. For more information, see [Managing environments for deployment](/en/actions/how-tos/deploy/configure-and-manage-deployments/manage-environments).
## Bypassing deployment protection rules
If you have configured deployment protection rules that control whether software can be deployed to an environment, you can bypass these rules and force all pending jobs referencing the environment to proceed.
> [!NOTE]
>
> * You cannot bypass deployment protection rules if the environment has been configured to prevent admins from bypassing configured protection rules. For more information, see [Managing environments for deployment](/en/actions/how-tos/deploy/configure-and-manage-deployments/manage-environments#creating-an-environment).
> * You can only bypass deployment protection rules during workflow execution when a job referencing the environment is in a "Pending" state.
1. Navigate to the workflow run. For more information about navigating to a workflow run, see [Viewing workflow run history](/en/actions/how-tos/monitor-workflows/view-workflow-run-history).
2. To the right of **Deployment protection rules**, click **Start all waiting jobs**.

# GITHUB_TOKEN
Learn what GITHUB_TOKEN is, how it works, and why it matters for secure automation in GitHub Actions workflows.
## About the `GITHUB_TOKEN`
At the start of each workflow job, GitHub automatically creates a unique `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret to use in your workflow. You can use the `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate in the workflow job.
When you enable GitHub Actions, GitHub installs a GitHub App on your repository. The `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret is a GitHub App installation access token. You can use the installation access token to authenticate on behalf of the GitHub App installed on your repository. The token's permissions are limited to the repository that contains your workflow. For more information, see [Workflow syntax for GitH
Before each job begins, GitHub fetches an installation access token for the job. The `GITHUB_TOKEN` expires when the job finishes or after its effective maximum lifetime.
The effective maximum lifetime of the token depends on the type of runner:
* **GitHub-hosted runners** The maximum job execution time is 6 hours, so the `GITHUB_TOKEN` can live for a maximum of 6 hours.
* **Self-hosted runners** The maximum job execution time is 5 days. However, because the `GITHUB_TOKEN` is an installation access token, it can only be refreshed for up to 24 hours. If your job runs longer than 24 hours, use a personal access token or other authentication method instead.
The token is also available in the `github.token` context. For more information, see [Contexts reference](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/contexts#github-context).
## When `GITHUB_TOKEN` triggers workflow runs
When you use the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN` to perform tasks, events triggered by the `GITHUB_TOKEN` will not create a new workflow run, with the following exceptions:
* `workflow_dispatch` and `repository_dispatch` events always create workflow runs.
* `pull_request` events with the `opened`, `synchronize`, or `reopened` activity types: when a workflow using `GITHUB_TOKEN` creates or updates a pull request, the resulting `pull_request` event creates workflow runs in an **approval-required** state. The pull request displays a banner in the merge box, and a user with write access to the repository can start the runs by selecting **Approve workfl
For all other events, this behavior prevents you from accidentally creating recursive workflow runs. For example, if a workflow run pushes code using the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, a new workflow will not run even when the repository contains a workflow configured to run when `push` events occur.
> [!NOTE]
> If you need workflow runs from workflow-created pull requests to execute without requiring approval, use a GitHub App installation access token or a personal access token instead of `GITHUB_TOKEN` when creating or updating the pull request.
Commits pushed by a GitHub Actions workflow that uses the `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not trigger a GitHub Pages build.
## Next steps
* [Use GITHUB\_TOKEN for authentication in workflows](/en/actions/tutorials/authenticate-with-github_token)

| 3.3.4 | **Inference — the agent loophole.** "Author" means the GitHub account that opened the PR.
- **Claude Code on a laptop** that opens the PR with the engineer's own `gh` login: the engineer is the author and cannot approve it (3.3.1). A second human is needed. This case is covered.
- **Claude GitHub App / `claude-code-action`** opening the PR: the **author is the app**. The engineer who triggered it is **not** blocked from approving, because GitHub's protection covers Copilot only (3.3.2). One approval could then mean zero independent reviewers.

  - require 2 approvals on protected branches;
  - path-based required reviewers (3.2.4);
  - "approval from someone other than the last person to push" (3.2.3), which does not help when the app is the last pusher and the triggering engineer approves;

### 3.6 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)

These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:

1. **The GitHub plan decides where the "named human approved it" gate can sit.**
   - **On Enterprise Cloud:** a `production` environment with required reviewers, prevent
     self-review, no admin bypass, and deployment branches = `main` (3.1.1–3.1.4). The approval
     is per deployment and logged as `workflows.approve_workflow_job` (3.5.6).
   - **On Team:** environments have **no approval gate** on a private repo (3.1.2). The gate must
     be the **PR merge to `main`**, enforced by:
     - rulesets: PR required, ≥1–2 approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for
       `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, last-push approval, no bypass;
     - the `production` environment restricted to `main` (3.1.3), so that only merged, approved
       code can get prod credentials.

     Merge approval then equals deploy approval. That works only if the deploy is automatic from
     `main`, and no one can run the deploy workflow on another ref.
   - **GĐ-5 is wrong unless Papaya is on Enterprise.** This should go back to the framing as a
     correction and an open question for Papaya.
2. **OIDC trust must pin both the repository and the gate** (3.4.2–3.4.5):
   - Prod roles trust only `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:production`, in the format the repo
     uses (3.4.4).
   - The environment allows only `main` (3.1.3).
   - Optionally, `job_workflow_ref` limits access to one reviewed reusable deploy workflow
     (3.4.5).
   - Non-prod roles trust a separate environment.
   - This removes the long-lived AWS keys from the brief (P5).
3. **Agent-authored PRs need one more rule than human PRs** (3.3.4). Opening PRs with the
   engineer's own identity keeps GitHub's built-in author rule. App-authored PRs need 2 approvals
   or a custom check. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" stays **off**
   (3.3.3).
4. **CI agents and policy files:** on GitHub-hosted runners the agent has root, so Claude Code
   managed settings written in the job are advisory (3.5.1, closes the Topic 1 question). The
   real limits for a CI agent are the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions (3.5.3), the absence of
   prod OIDC trust for that job (no `production` environment), and the base-branch config restore
   in `claude-code-action` (1.7.9). Self-hosted runners would allow a root-owned policy, but bring
   persistence risks (3.5.2).
5. **Supply chain of CI itself:**
   - Workflow lockfile or SHA pinning, enforced by org policy (3.5.5).
   - CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8), plus CI validation of the CODEOWNERS file, because invalid
     lines fail silently (3.2.7).
   - Restricted default `GITHUB_TOKEN` (3.5.3); no `pull_request_target` with checkout (3.5.4).
6. **Audit retention gap:** the org audit log keeps 180 days (3.5.6). ISO 27001 and HIPAA
   evidence needs longer, so the audit log must be exported or streamed. Streaming was not
   researched (⚠️; it may be Enterprise-only).

- **Claude Code on a laptop** that opens the PR with the engineer's own `gh` login: the engineer is the author and cannot approve it (3.3.1). A second human is needed. This case is covered.
- **Claude GitHub App / `claude-code-action`** opening the PR: the **author is the app**. The engineer who triggered it is **not** blocked from approving, because GitHub's protection covers Copilot only (3.3.2). One approval could then mean zero independent reviewers.

  - require 2 approvals on protected branches;
  - path-based required reviewers (3.2.4);
  - "approval from someone other than the last person to push" (3.2.3), which does not help when the app is the last pusher and the triggering engineer approves;

### 3.6 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)

These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:

1. **The GitHub plan decides where the "named human approved it" gate can sit.**
   - **On Enterprise Cloud:** a `production` environment with required reviewers, prevent
     self-review, no admin bypass, and deployment branches = `main` (3.1.1–3.1.4). The approval
     is per deployment and logged as `workflows.approve_workflow_job` (3.5.6).
   - **On Team:** environments have **no approval gate** on a private repo (3.1.2). The gate must
     be the **PR merge to `main`**, enforced by:
     - rulesets: PR required, ≥1–2 approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for
       `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, last-push approval, no bypass;
     - the `production` environment restricted to `main` (3.1.3), so that only merged, approved
       code can get prod credentials.

     Merge approval then equals deploy approval. That works only if the deploy is automatic from
     `main`, and no one can run the deploy workflow on another ref.
   - **GĐ-5 is wrong unless Papaya is on Enterprise.** This should go back to the framing as a
     correction and an open question for Papaya.
2. **OIDC trust must pin both the repository and the gate** (3.4.2–3.4.5):
   - Prod roles trust only `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:production`, in the format the repo
     uses (3.4.4).
   - The environment allows only `main` (3.1.3).
   - Optionally, `job_workflow_ref` limits access to one reviewed reusable deploy workflow
     (3.4.5).
   - Non-prod roles trust a separate environment.
   - This removes the long-lived AWS keys from the brief (P5).
3. **Agent-authored PRs need one more rule than human PRs** (3.3.4). Opening PRs with the
   engineer's own identity keeps GitHub's built-in author rule. App-authored PRs need 2 approvals
   or a custom check. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" stays **off**
   (3.3.3).
4. **CI agents and policy files:** on GitHub-hosted runners the agent has root, so Claude Code
   managed settings written in the job are advisory (3.5.1, closes the Topic 1 question). The
   real limits for a CI agent are the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions (3.5.3), the absence of
   prod OIDC trust for that job (no `production` environment), and the base-branch config restore
   in `claude-code-action` (1.7.9). Self-hosted runners would allow a root-owned policy, but bring
   persistence risks (3.5.2).
5. **Supply chain of CI itself:**
   - Workflow lockfile or SHA pinning, enforced by org policy (3.5.5).
   - CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8), plus CI validation of the CODEOWNERS file, because invalid
     lines fail silently (3.2.7).
   - Restricted default `GITHUB_TOKEN` (3.5.3); no `pull_request_target` with checkout (3.5.4).
6. **Audit retention gap:** the org audit log keeps 180 days (3.5.6). ISO 27001 and HIPAA
   evidence needs longer, so the audit log must be exported or streamed. Streaming was not
   researched (⚠️; it may be Enterprise-only).

- With an environment: `repo:ORG/REPO:environment:NAME`. Otherwise: `…:ref:refs/heads/BRANCH`, `…:ref:refs/tags/TAG`, or `…:pull_request`.
- "If you use a workflow with an environment, the `sub` field must reference the environment name".
- **Inference:** the environment form **does not contain the branch**. Which branches may use the role is then enforced only by the environment's deployment-branch rule (3.1.3), not by AWS.

| ✅ / ⚠️ (inference) | [oidc reference: example subject claims](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/oidc#example-subject-claims), [oidc-in-aws](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/security-harden-deployments/oidc-in-aws) |

Older repositories keep the old format "unless you opt in". | 3.4.5 | The subject can be customised per org or repo with `include_claim_keys`, for example to require `job_workflow_ref`, so that only a specific **reusable workflow** at a specific ref can get the role (`repo:…:environment:prod:job_workflow_ref:…`). "Support for custom claims for OIDC is unavailable in AWS". This refers to custom claims beyond `sub`; a customised **`sub`** still works with AWS's `:sub` condition. It "only enables fetching and setting the OIDC token; it does not grant write access to other resources". | ✅ | [oidc reference: workflow permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/oidc#workflow-permissions-for-the-requesting-the-oidc-token) |

### 3.5 Runners, tokens, third-party actions, audit

| # | Finding | Marker | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.5.1 | **GitHub-hosted runners:** "The Linux and macOS virtual machines both run using passwordless `sudo`". Each runner, except single-CPU ones, "is a new virtual machine". The Actions security guide calls them "ephemeral and clean isolated virtual machines". **This answers Topic 1 open item (1.9 / 1.8 #3):** a step running an agent on a GitHub-hosted runner can rewrite `/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json` via `sudo`. A policy file written by an earlier step in the same job is **not** tamper-proof against the agent step. | ✅ | [github-hosted-runners: administrative privileges](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners#administrative-privileges), [secure-use](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use) |
| 3.5.2 | **Self-hosted runners:** "do not have guarantees around running in ephemeral clean virtual machines, and can be persistently compromised by untrusted code". Anyone who can open a PR in a private repo "generally those with read access" can compromise them. Runner groups limit which repositories can use them. Just-in-time runners exist (not read in detail, 📖). | ✅ | [secure-use: hardening for self-hosted runners](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use) |
| 3.5.3 | `GITHUB_TOKEN` is a GitHub App installation token "limited to the repository that contains your workflow". It lives at most 6 hours on hosted runners. The default org or repository setting is either "permissive" (read and write for all) or "restricted" (read for `contents` and `packages`). Per-job `permissions:` narrows it. | ✅ | [github_token](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/github_token), [disabling-or-limiting-github-actions-for-your-organization](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-organization-settings/disabling-or-limiting-github-actions-for-your-organization) |
| 3.5.4 | `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run` "are privileged" and "may have repository write access and access to referenced secrets". They must not check out untrusted code. | ✅ | [secure-use: untrusted code checkout](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use) |
| 3.5.5 | **Third-party actions:** a compromised action "would have access to all secrets configured on your repository". The strongest measure is a **workflow dependency lockfile** (`.github/workflows/actions.lock`, generated by `gh actions-lock`). It "pins a commit SHA to every action … including transitive dependencies" but does not pin reusable workflows. The alternative is full-SHA pinning. There is an org policy "Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA", and locked dependencies satisfy it. | ✅ | [secure-use: third-party actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use), [workflow-dependency-lockfiles](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/workflow-dependency-lockfiles), [disabling-or-limiting-github-actions-for-your-organization](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-organization-settings/disabling-or-limiting-github-actions-for-your-organization) |

- It covers "the last 180 days", and "only owners can access" it.
- Events include `workflows.approve_workflow_job` (a deployment approval), `environment.update_protection_rule`, `repository_ruleset.create/update/destroy`, `protected_branch.policy_override`, and `org.update_actions_secret`.
- Many events carry an `actor_is_agent` field. **Its meaning is not defined** in the pages read (⚠️).

| ✅ / ⚠️ (`actor_is_agent`) | [reviewing-the-audit-log-for-your-organization](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/keeping-your-organization-secure/managing-security-settings-for-your-organization/reviewing-the-audit-log-for-your-organization), [audit-log-events](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/keeping-your-organization-secure/managing-security-settings-for-your-organization/audit-log-events-for-your-organization) |

### 3.6 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)

These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:

1. **The GitHub plan decides where the "named human approved it" gate can sit.**
   - **On Enterprise Cloud:** a `production` environment with required reviewers, prevent
     self-review, no admin bypass, and deployment branches = `main` (3.1.1–3.1.4). The approval
     is per deployment and logged as `workflows.approve_workflow_job` (3.5.6).
   - **On Team:** environments have **no approval gate** on a private repo (3.1.2). The gate must
     be the **PR merge to `main`**, enforced by:
     - rulesets: PR required, ≥1–2 approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for
       `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, last-push approval, no bypass;
     - the `production` environment restricted to `main` (3.1.3), so that only merged, approved
       code can get prod credentials.

     Merge approval then equals deploy approval. That works only if the deploy is automatic from
     `main`, and no one can run the deploy workflow on another ref.
   - **GĐ-5 is wrong unless Papaya is on Enterprise.** This should go back to the framing as a
     correction and an open question for Papaya.
2. **OIDC trust must pin both the repository and the gate** (3.4.2–3.4.5):
   - Prod roles trust only `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:production`, in the format the repo
     uses (3.4.4).
   - The environment allows only `main` (3.1.3).
   - Optionally, `job_workflow_ref` limits access to one reviewed reusable deploy workflow
     (3.4.5).
   - Non-prod roles trust a separate environment.
   - This removes the long-lived AWS keys from the brief (P5).
3. **Agent-authored PRs need one more rule than human PRs** (3.3.4). Opening PRs with the
   engineer's own identity keeps GitHub's built-in author rule. App-authored PRs need 2 approvals
   or a custom check. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" stays **off**
   (3.3.3).
4. **CI agents and policy files:** on GitHub-hosted runners the agent has root, so Claude Code
   managed settings written in the job are advisory (3.5.1, closes the Topic 1 question). The
   real limits for a CI agent are the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions (3.5.3), the absence of
   prod OIDC trust for that job (no `production` environment), and the base-branch config restore
   in `claude-code-action` (1.7.9). Self-hosted runners would allow a root-owned policy, but bring
   persistence risks (3.5.2).
5. **Supply chain of CI itself:**
   - Workflow lockfile or SHA pinning, enforced by org policy (3.5.5).
   - CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8), plus CI validation of the CODEOWNERS file, because invalid
     lines fail silently (3.2.7).
   - Restricted default `GITHUB_TOKEN` (3.5.3); no `pull_request_target` with checkout (3.5.4).
6. **Audit retention gap:** the org audit log keeps 180 days (3.5.6). ISO 27001 and HIPAA
   evidence needs longer, so the audit log must be exported or streamed. Streaming was not
   researched (⚠️; it may be Enterprise-only).

### 3.7 Open items (Topic 3)

- [ ] ⚠️ **Papaya's GitHub plan** (Team vs Enterprise Cloud). It decides 3.6 #1 and corrects GĐ-5.
- [ ] ⚠️ Default admin-bypass behaviour for environments on Team private repos (3.1.4).
- [ ] ⚠️ Which plans allow OIDC subject customisation (3.4.5), and whether Papaya's monorepo uses
      the old or the immutable `sub` format (3.4.4).
- [ ] ⚠️ Audit-log streaming or export, and its plan (3.6 #6). Meaning of `actor_is_agent` (3.5.6).
- [ ] ⚠️ How the Claude GitHub App attributes PRs and commits, and whether the triggering human is

new='''### 3.6 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)

These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:

1. **The GitHub plan decides where the "named human approved it" gate can sit.**
   - **On Enterprise Cloud:** a `production` environment with required reviewers, prevent
     self-review, no admin bypass, and deployment branches = `main` (3.1.1–3.1.4). The approval
     is per deployment job and logged as `workflows.approve_workflow_job` (3.5.6).
   - **On Team:** environments have **no approval gate** on a private repo (3.1.2). The gate must
     be the **PR merge to `main`**, enforced by:
     - rulesets: PR required, ≥1–2 approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for
       `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, last-push approval, an empty bypass
       list (3.2.2–3.2.4);
     - the `production` environment restricted to `main` (3.1.3).
   - **Prerequisite on both plans: the branch rule alone does not mean "only merged, approved
     code reaches prod".** Every workflow on `main` passes a "main only" rule, whatever its trigger
     (3.4.5c). So all of the following must also hold:
     - only reviewed deploy workflows may reference `production`, enforced by CODEOWNERS on
       `.github/workflows` and a CI check;
     - deploy workflows take no ref or SHA input, and deploy the commit they run on;
     - no `production` job runs on `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run`;
     - preferably, the `sub` claim is pinned to the reusable deploy workflow (`job_workflow_ref`,
       3.4.5).

     Under these conditions, merge approval equals deploy approval on Team.
   - **Admins remain a gap.** Admins and holders of "edit repository rules" can edit rulesets,
     environments and the OIDC `sub` customisation. This is logged, not prevented (3.1.4, 3.2.2,
     3.4.5). So: few admins, periodic access review, and alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`,
     `environment.update_protection_rule` and `protected_branch.policy_override`.
   - **GĐ-5 holds only on Enterprise.** It should go back to the framing as a correction and an
     open question for Papaya.
2. **OIDC trust must pin the repository, the gate and, where possible, the workflow** (3.4.2–3.4.5c):
   - **AWS:** prod roles trust only `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:production`, in the repo's
     `sub` format (3.4.4). Ideally a customised `sub` includes `job_workflow_ref`, because AWS
     cannot test other claims (3.4.5).
   - **GCP:** the attribute condition must restrict to the GitHub organization (required by
     Google). It can also test `job_workflow_ref`, `ref` and `event_name` directly (3.4.5b).
   - **Non-prod:** roles trust a separate environment.
   - **Secrets:** prod credentials never live in repository secrets, because anyone with write
     access can read those (3.5.6). This removes the long-lived AWS keys from the brief (P5).
3. **Agent-authored PRs need one more rule than human PRs** (3.3.4). Opening PRs with the
   engineer's own identity keeps GitHub's built-in author rule. App-authored PRs need 2 approvals
   or a custom check whose source app is pinned. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull
   requests" stays **off** (3.3.3).
4. **CI agents and policy files:** on standard GitHub-hosted runners, an agent with shell access
   has root, so Claude Code managed settings written in the job are advisory (3.5.1, closes the
   Topic 1 question). The real limits for a CI agent are:
   - the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions (3.5.3);
   - **no** `environment: production` in any agent workflow, so it gets no prod OIDC trust
     (3.4.5c);
   - the base-branch config restore in `claude-code-action` (1.7.9).

   Self-hosted runners would allow a root-owned policy, but bring persistence risks (3.5.2).
5. **Supply chain of CI itself:**
   - Workflow lockfile or SHA pinning, enforced by org policy (3.5.5).
   - CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8), plus CI validation of the CODEOWNERS file, because invalid
     lines fail silently (3.2.7).
   - Restricted default `GITHUB_TOKEN` (3.5.3); no `pull_request_target` with checkout (3.5.4).
6. **Audit retention gap:** the org audit log keeps 180 days (3.5.6). ISO 27001 and HIPAA evidence
   needs longer, so it must be exported periodically (JSON or CSV, within the export limits, ✅)
   or streamed (⚠️ not researched; may be Enterprise-only).

### 3.7 Open items (Topic 3)

- [ ] ⚠️ **Papaya's GitHub plan** (Team vs Enterprise Cloud). It decides 3.6 #1 and corrects GĐ-5.
- [ ] ⚠️ On Team private repos, can admins bypass or simply edit the environment branch
      restriction (3.1.4)? Are org-level rulesets available on Team (3.2.1, the docs contradict
      each other)?
- [ ] ⚠️ Which plans allow OIDC subject customisation (3.4.5), and whether Papaya's monorepo uses

Giả định của mình (giữ nguyên ý, không tự đổi):
1. Gói GitHub: giả định Papaya dùng gói Team (không phải Enterprise).
2. Format `sub` của OIDC: giả định repo dùng format mới (có ID). Mình không biết ngày tạo repo thật của Papaya.
3. Claude GitHub App: mình chưa biết nó ghi tác giả PR và commit thế nào. Giả định xấu nhất: tác giả PR là app, người gọi agent vẫn tự duyệt được. Thiết kế không được dựa vào hành vi mặc định của app.
4. Merge queue : Giả định là có sử dụng merge queue, thiết kế cần chạy được với merge queue thì chỉ ghi rõ cần thêm gì, đừng đổi giả định.

Việc cần làm:
1. Trong mục 3.7, ghi 4 giả định trên dưới tiêu đề "Giả định của owner" kèm ngày, đánh dấu rõ là giả định, không phải sự thật về Papaya. Giữ nguyên các câu hỏi để hỏi Papaya nếu có cơ hội.
2. Cập nhật giả định GĐ-5 trong work/01-problem-framing.md cho khớp với giả định gói Team, và nói rõ đã đổi gì.
3. Với từng giả định, ghi hệ quả cho thiết kế: giả định Team thì cổng duyệt đặt ở merge PR vào main bằng rulesets; giả định `sub` mới thì trust policy phải khớp format đó; giả định app là tác giả thì cần 2 approval hoặc status check pin app nguồn. Chỗ nào rẻ để thiết kế bao phủ cả hai trường hợp (ví dụ Enterprise nếu Papaya nâng gói sau này) thì ghi thêm một dòng, nhưng không đổi giả định nền.
4. Không sửa các kết luận đã qua review ở 3.1 đến 3.6, trừ khi giả định của mình làm kết luận đó sai; nếu có thì nêu cụ thể cho mình quyết.
5. Thêm một dòng vào nhật ký review ghi việc vừa làm và ai quyết định.
6. Cho mình xem diff trước khi commit.
Mình đọc lại mục 3.7, GĐ-5, và trang merge queue trước khi ghi. Giả định 1 (gói Team) và giả định 4 (dùng merge queue) có thể vướng nhau về gói.

input.new_string:
### 3.7 Open items (Topic 3)

#### Giả định của owner (2026-11-08)

**These are design assumptions set by the repo owner, not facts about Papaya.** The owner has no
access to Papaya's systems. Recorded verbatim, as written by the owner in the session of
2026-11-08:

> 1. Gói GitHub: giả định Papaya dùng gói Team (không phải Enterprise).
> 2. Format `sub` của OIDC: giả định repo dùng format mới (có ID). Mình không biết ngày tạo repo thật của Papaya.
> 3. Claude GitHub App: mình chưa biết nó ghi tác giả PR và commit thế nào. Giả định xấu nhất: tác giả PR là app, người gọi agent vẫn tự duyệt được. Thiết kế không được dựa vào hành vi mặc định của app.
> 4. Merge queue : Giả định là có sử dụng merge queue, thiết kế cần chạy được với merge queue thì chỉ ghi rõ cần thêm gì, đừng đổi giả định.

**Consequences for the design.** These are my inferences from 3.1–3.6, unless a source is given.
The "cheap to cover the other case" lines do not change the assumptions.

| Assumption | Consequence for the design | Cheap to cover the other case |
|---|---|---|
| A1 — GitHub **Team** | Environment approval gates are unavailable on the private monorepo (3.1.2). **The approval gate is the PR merge to `main`, enforced by rulesets** (3.2.1–3.2.4): PR required, approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, approval after the last push, and an empty bypass list. The `production` environment is restricted to `main` (3.1.3). All the prerequisites in 3.6 #1 apply: only reviewed deploy workflows reference `production`, deploys take no ref input, and no privileged triggers are used. Admin edits are logged, not prevented. Drift detection is needed (3.1.4, 3.6 #1). | Create the `production` environment now, with the branch restriction. If Papaya moves to Enterprise Cloud, add required reviewers, prevent self-review, and disallow admin bypass on that environment. This is a settings change only; the workflows and the OIDC trust stay the same (inference). |
| A2 — immutable `sub` (with IDs) | AWS and GCP trust conditions must match `repo:<owner>@<owner-id>/<repo>@<repo-id>:environment:production`, with placeholders in `examples/` (3.4.4). If the `sub` is customised with `job_workflow_ref` (3.4.5), the IDs stay in the `repo` segment and cannot be removed (3.4.4, oidc reference). | The org or repo can **opt in** to immutable subject claims (3.4.4). Opting in makes A2 true regardless of the repo's creation date. Accepting the old format as well would bring back the namespace-recycling risk, so it is not recommended. |
| A3 — worst case: the app is the PR author, and the person who triggered the agent can approve | The built-in "authors cannot approve" rule cannot be relied on (3.3.1, 3.3.4). Protected branches need **2 approvals**, at least on paths an agent can change, **or** a required status check whose **expected source app is pinned** (3.2.5, 3.3.4). The check fails when the approver is the person who triggered the agent run. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" stays off (3.3.3). Agent workflows never reference `production` (3.6 #4). | These rules still hold, and cost little, if the app turns out to attribute PRs to the human. |
| A4 — merge queue in use | Workflows that report required checks **must also trigger on `merge_group`**: "You **must** use the `merge_group` event to trigger your GitHub Actions workflow when a pull request is added to a merge queue" ([managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue), ✅). `merge_group` runs carry the merge-group ref (3.4.5c), so a `production` environment restricted to `main` does not serve them. That is the intended result: queue runs are CI only, and the deploy runs on `main` after the queue merges. PRs must pass the required protections before a user "can add the pull request to the queue" (same page, ✅). ⚠️ Not verified: that the queue's merge to `main` triggers `push` workflows as a normal merge does. | Adding `merge_group` triggers does no harm in a repo without a queue. |

**Conflict between A1 and A4, for the owner to decide.** I have not changed either assumption.
- The merge queue page says: "Pull request merge queues are available in any public repository
  owned by an organization, or in private repositories owned by organizations using GitHub
  Enterprise Cloud" (plan banner of
  [managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue),
  ✅).
- So on the **Team** plan, a **private** monorepo cannot use a merge queue. A1 and A4 cannot both
  hold.
- The design above works under either one, because nothing in it depends on the queue. The only
  difference is whether `merge_group` triggers are needed.

**Questions to ask Papaya if there is a chance** (the open items below remain open; the owner's
assumptions do not answer them):

- [ ] ⚠️ **Papaya's GitHub plan** (Team vs Enterprise Cloud). It decides 3.6 #1 and corrects GĐ-5.
      *Design assumption: Team (A1).*

**Thay đổi GĐ-5 (2026-11-08):**
- **Trước:** "Gói GitHub của Papaya hỗ trợ environment protection rules (required reviewers) cho private repo", chưa kiểm tra.
- **Kiểm tra docs** (`work/02-research.md` 3.1.2): tính năng này trên repo private chỉ có ở Enterprise.
- **Quyết định của owner:** giả định gói **Team**. Đây là giả định để thiết kế, không phải sự thật về Papaya.

### 3.7 Open items (Topic 3)

#### Giả định của owner (2026-11-08)

**These are design assumptions set by the repo owner, not facts about Papaya.** The owner has no
access to Papaya's systems. Recorded verbatim, as written by the owner in the session of
2026-11-08:

> 1. Gói GitHub: giả định Papaya dùng gói Team (không phải Enterprise).
> 2. Format `sub` của OIDC: giả định repo dùng format mới (có ID). Mình không biết ngày tạo repo thật của Papaya.
> 3. Claude GitHub App: mình chưa biết nó ghi tác giả PR và commit thế nào. Giả định xấu nhất: tác giả PR là app, người gọi agent vẫn tự duyệt được. Thiết kế không được dựa vào hành vi mặc định của app.
> 4. Merge queue : Giả định là có sử dụng merge queue, thiết kế cần chạy được với merge queue thì chỉ ghi rõ cần thêm gì, đừng đổi giả định.

**Consequences for the design.** These are my inferences from 3.1–3.6, unless a source is given.
The "cheap to cover the other case" lines do not change the assumptions.

| Assumption | Consequence for the design | Cheap to cover the other case |
|---|---|---|
| A1 — GitHub **Team** | Environment approval gates are unavailable on the private monorepo (3.1.2). **The approval gate is the PR merge to `main`, enforced by rulesets** (3.2.1–3.2.4): PR required, approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, approval after the last push, and an empty bypass list. The `production` environment is restricted to `main` (3.1.3). All the prerequisites in 3.6 #1 apply: only reviewed deploy workflows reference `production`, deploys take no ref input, and no privileged triggers are used. Admin edits are logged, not prevented. Drift detection is needed (3.1.4, 3.6 #1). | Create the `production` environment now, with the branch restriction. If Papaya moves to Enterprise Cloud, add required reviewers, prevent self-review, and disallow admin bypass on that environment. This is a settings change only; the workflows and the OIDC trust stay the same (inference). |
| A2 — immutable `sub` (with IDs) | AWS and GCP trust conditions must match `repo:<owner>@<owner-id>/<repo>@<repo-id>:environment:production`, with placeholders in `examples/` (3.4.4). If the `sub` is customised with `job_workflow_ref` (3.4.5), the IDs stay in the `repo` segment and cannot be removed (3.4.4, oidc reference). | The org or repo can **opt in** to immutable subject claims (3.4.4). Opting in makes A2 true regardless of the repo's creation date. Accepting the old format as well would bring back the namespace-recycling risk, so it is not recommended. |
| A3 — worst case: the app is the PR author, and the person who triggered the agent can approve | The built-in "authors cannot approve" rule cannot be relied on (3.3.1, 3.3.4). Protected branches need **2 approvals**, at least on paths an agent can change, **or** a required status check whose **expected source app is pinned** (3.2.5, 3.3.4). The check fails when the approver is the person who triggered the agent run. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" stays off (3.3.3). Agent workflows never reference `production` (3.6 #4). | These rules still hold, and cost little, if the app turns out to attribute PRs to the human. |
| A4 — merge queue in use | Workflows that report required checks **must also trigger on `merge_group`**: "You **must** use the `merge_group` event to trigger your GitHub Actions workflow when a pull request is added to a merge queue" ([managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue), ✅). `merge_group` runs carry the merge-group ref (3.4.5c), so a `production` environment restricted to `main` does not serve them. That is the intended result: queue runs are CI only, and the deploy runs on `main` after the queue merges. PRs must pass the required protections before a user "can add the pull request to the queue" (same page, ✅). ⚠️ Not verified: that the queue's merge to `main` triggers `push` workflows as a normal merge does. | Adding `merge_group` triggers does no harm in a repo without a queue. |

**Conflict between A1 and A4, for the owner to decide.** I have not changed either assumption.
- The merge queue page says: "Pull request merge queues are available in any public repository
  owned by an organization, or in private repositories owned by organizations using GitHub
  Enterprise Cloud" (plan banner of
  [managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue),
  ✅).
- So on the **Team** plan, a **private** monorepo cannot use a merge queue. A1 and A4 cannot both
  hold.
- The design above works under either one, because nothing in it depends on the queue. The only
  difference is whether `merge_group` triggers are needed.

**Questions to ask Papaya if there is a chance** (the open items below remain open; the owner's
assumptions do not answer them):

- [ ] ⚠️ **Papaya's GitHub plan** (Team vs Enterprise Cloud). It decides 3.6 #1 and corrects GĐ-5.
      *Design assumption: Team (A1).*

### 3.7 Open items (Topic 3)

#### Giả định của owner (2026-11-08)

**These are design assumptions set by the repo owner, not facts about Papaya.** The owner has no
access to Papaya's systems. Recorded verbatim, as written by the owner in the session of
2026-11-08:

> 1. Gói GitHub: giả định Papaya dùng gói Team (không phải Enterprise).
> 2. Format `sub` của OIDC: giả định repo dùng format mới (có ID). Mình không biết ngày tạo repo thật của Papaya.
> 3. Claude GitHub App: mình chưa biết nó ghi tác giả PR và commit thế nào. Giả định xấu nhất: tác giả PR là app, người gọi agent vẫn tự duyệt được. Thiết kế không được dựa vào hành vi mặc định của app.
> 4. Merge queue : Giả định là có sử dụng merge queue, thiết kế cần chạy được với merge queue thì chỉ ghi rõ cần thêm gì, đừng đổi giả định.

**Consequences for the design.** These are my inferences from 3.1–3.6, unless a source is given.
The "cheap to cover the other case" lines do not change the assumptions.

| Assumption | Consequence for the design | Cheap to cover the other case |
|---|---|---|
| A1 — GitHub **Team** | Environment approval gates are unavailable on the private monorepo (3.1.2). **The approval gate is the PR merge to `main`, enforced by rulesets** (3.2.1–3.2.4): PR required, approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, approval after the last push, and an empty bypass list. The `production` environment is restricted to `main` (3.1.3). All the prerequisites in 3.6 #1 apply: only reviewed deploy workflows reference `production`, deploys take no ref input, and no privileged triggers are used. Admin edits are logged, not prevented. Drift detection is needed (3.1.4, 3.6 #1). | Create the `production` environment now, with the branch restriction. If Papaya moves to Enterprise Cloud, add required reviewers, prevent self-review, and disallow admin bypass on that environment. This is a settings change only; the workflows and the OIDC trust stay the same (inference). |
| A2 — immutable `sub` (with IDs) | AWS and GCP trust conditions must match `repo:<owner>@<owner-id>/<repo>@<repo-id>:environment:production`, with placeholders in `examples/` (3.4.4). If the `sub` is customised with `job_workflow_ref` (3.4.5), the IDs stay in the `repo` segment and cannot be removed (3.4.4, oidc reference). | The org or repo can **opt in** to immutable subject claims (3.4.4). Opting in makes A2 true regardless of the repo's creation date. Accepting the old format as well would bring back the namespace-recycling risk, so it is not recommended. |
| A3 — worst case: the app is the PR author, and the person who triggered the agent can approve | The built-in "authors cannot approve" rule cannot be relied on (3.3.1, 3.3.4). Protected branches need **2 approvals**, at least on paths an agent can change, **or** a required status check whose **expected source app is pinned** (3.2.5, 3.3.4). The check fails when the approver is the person who triggered the agent run. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" stays off (3.3.3). Agent workflows never reference `production` (3.6 #4). | These rules still hold, and cost little, if the app turns out to attribute PRs to the human. |
| A4 — merge queue in use | Workflows that report required checks **must also trigger on `merge_group`**: "You **must** use the `merge_group` event to trigger your GitHub Actions workflow when a pull request is added to a merge queue" ([managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue), ✅). `merge_group` runs carry the merge-group ref (3.4.5c), so a `production` environment restricted to `main` does not serve them. That is the intended result: queue runs are CI only, and the deploy runs on `main` after the queue merges. PRs must pass the required protections before a user "can add the pull request to the queue" (same page, ✅). ⚠️ Not verified: that the queue's merge to `main` triggers `push` workflows as a normal merge does. | Adding `merge_group` triggers does no harm in a repo without a queue. |

**Conflict between A1 and A4, for the owner to decide.** I have not changed either assumption.
- The merge queue page says: "Pull request merge queues are available in any public repository
  owned by an organization, or in private repositories owned by organizations using GitHub
  Enterprise Cloud" (plan banner of
  [managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue),
  ✅).
- So on the **Team** plan, a **private** monorepo cannot use a merge queue. A1 and A4 cannot both
  hold.
- The design above works under either one, because nothing in it depends on the queue. The only
  difference is whether `merge_group` triggers are needed.

+### 3.7 Open items (Topic 3)
+
+#### Giả định của owner (2026-11-08)
+
+**These are design assumptions set by the repo owner, not facts about Papaya.** The owner has no
+access to Papaya's systems. Recorded verbatim, as written by the owner in the session of
+2026-11-08:
+
+> 1. Gói GitHub: giả định Papaya dùng gói Team (không phải Enterprise).
+> 2. Format `sub` của OIDC: giả định repo dùng format mới (có ID). Mình không biết ngày tạo repo thật của Papaya.
+> 3. Claude GitHub App: mình chưa biết nó ghi tác giả PR và commit thế nào. Giả định xấu nhất: tác giả PR là app, người gọi agent vẫn tự duyệt được. Thiết kế không được dựa vào hành vi mặc định của app.
+> 4. Merge queue : Giả định là có sử dụng merge queue, thiết kế cần chạy được với merge queue thì chỉ ghi rõ cần thêm gì, đừng đổi giả định.
+
+**Consequences for the design.** These are my inferences from 3.1–3.6, unless a source is given.
+The "cheap to cover the other case" lines do not change the assumptions.
+
+| Assumption | Consequence for the design | Cheap to cover the other case |
+|---|---|---|
+| A1 — GitHub **Team** | Environment approval gates are unavailable on the private monorepo (3.1.2). **The approval gate is the PR merge to `main`, enforced by rulesets** (3.2.1–3.2.4): PR required, approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, approval after the last push, and an empty bypass list. The `production` environme
+| A2 — immutable `sub` (with IDs) | AWS and GCP trust conditions must match `repo:<owner>@<owner-id>/<repo>@<repo-id>:environment:production` (inference from the documented `ref` examples), with placeholders in `examples/` (3.4.4). If the `sub` is customised with `job_workflow_ref` (3.4.5), the IDs stay in the `repo` segment and cannot be removed (3.4.4, oidc reference). | The org or repo can *
+| A3 — worst case: the app is the PR author, and the person who triggered the agent can approve | The built-in "authors cannot approve" rule cannot be relied on (3.3.1, 3.3.4). Protected branches need **2 approvals**, at least on paths an agent can change, **or** a required status check whose **expected source app is pinned** (3.2.5, 3.3.4). The check fails when the approver is the person who t
+| A4 — merge queue in use | Workflows that report required checks **must also trigger on `merge_group`**: "You **must** use the `merge_group` event to trigger your GitHub Actions workflow when a pull request is added to a merge queue" ([managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-me
+- (a) the A3 self-approval check, and every gate check, must also run on `merge_group` and evaluate **each PR in the group**. This means mapping the group back to its PRs and approvers (⚠️ design).
+- (b) enable "Only merge non-failing pull requests". When it is off, "Pull requests that have failed required checks can be added to a group as long as the last pull request in the group has passed" (same page, ✅). That would let a PR that failed the self-approval check through.
+- (c) turn on the "Require merge queue" setting. The queue page says it is "configured under branch protection rules or rulesets" ([about-protected-branches](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches), [managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merge
+
+**Audit evidence:** with a queue, the queue performs the merge, so the "merged by" actor may not be the approver (⚠️ not verified). Evidence for Compliance should come from the review approvals and the add-to-queue event. ⚠️ Also not verified: that the queue's merge to `main` triggers `push` workflows as a normal merge does. | Adding `merge_group` triggers does no harm in a repo without a
+
+**Conflict between A1 and A4, for the owner to decide.** I have not changed either assumption.
+- The merge queue page says: "Pull request merge queues are available in any public repository
+  owned by an organization, or in private repositories owned by organizations using GitHub
+  Enterprise Cloud" (plan banner of
+  [managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue),
+  ✅).
+- So on the **Team** plan, a **private** monorepo cannot use a merge queue. A1 and A4 cannot both
+  hold.
+- The design above works under either one, because nothing in it depends on the queue. The only
+  difference is whether `merge_group` triggers are needed.
+
+**Questions to ask Papaya if there is a chance** (the open items below remain open; the owner's
+assumptions do not answer them):
+
+- [ ] ⚠️ **Papaya's GitHub plan** (Team vs Enterprise Cloud). It decides 3.6 #1. *Design
+      assumption: Team (A1); GĐ-5 updated accordingly on 2026-11-08.*
+- [ ] ⚠️ On Team private repos, can admins bypass the environment branch restriction at run
+      time, and is a UI change to the branch policy audited (3.1.4)? Are org-level rulesets available on Team (3.2.1, the docs contradict
+      each other)?
+- [ ] ⚠️ Which plans allow OIDC subject customisation (3.4.5), and whether Papaya's monorepo uses
+      the old or the immutable `sub` format (3.4.4). *Design assumption: immutable (A2).*
+- [ ] ⚠️ Audit-log streaming and its plan; meaning of `actor_is_agent` (3.5.6).
+- [ ] ⚠️ How the Claude GitHub App attributes PRs and commits, whether the triggering human is
+      recorded anywhere usable for a self-approval check, and whether an approval from a GitHub
+      App counts toward required approvals (Copilot's does not, 3.3.1) (3.3.4). *Design
+      assumption: worst case (A3).*
+- [ ] ⚠️ Does Papaya use a merge queue? (`merge_group` runs carry the merge-group ref, 3.4.5c.)
+      *Design assumption: yes (A4); see the conflict with A1 above.*
+- [ ] ⚠️ Does sudo exist on single-CPU hosted runners (3.5.1)?

| 2.5.5 | **AWS MCP Server in CloudTrail:**
- "All AWS MCP Server actions for authenticated tools are logged by CloudTrail". An example is the `CallReadWriteTool` action, whose event includes an "Exact copy of MCP request params" **and** `responseElements.content[].text`, the tool output.
- The sample event has `"eventCategory": "Data"` and `"eventType": "AwsMcpEvent"`. Data events are off by default (2.6.3), and the CloudTrail data-event resource table (read today) has no `aws-mcp` resource type. Yet the MCP page also says the events appear in Event history, which shows only management events (2.6.1). **The docs are inconsistent here. -| 2.7.2 | **Database Activity Streams (Aurora PostgreSQL):** a near-real-time activity stream pushed to Kinesis, always encrypted with KMS. Separation from DBAs needs configuration: "you can control administrator access to data streams by configuring the Database Activity Streams feature. DBAs don't have access to the collection, transmission, storage, and processing of the streams".
- **Asynchronous mode:** records "might have been lost" during errors.
- **Synchronous mode:** the session waits until the record is durable, but "if the event can't be made durable for some reason, the database session returns to normal activities", and an RDS event says records might be lost.
- **Both modes:** loss is signalled by RDS events, which need an alert.
The rest of this row: It must be stopped before a major version upgrade. lines: > 3. Claude GitHub App: mình chưa biết nó ghi tác giả PR và commit thế nào. Giả định xấu nhất: tác giả PR là app, người gọi agent vẫn tự duyệt được. Thiết kế không được dựa vào hành vi mặc định của app.
> 4. Merge queue : Giả định là có sử dụng merge queue, thiết kế cần chạy được với merge queue thì chỉ ghi rõ cần thêm gì, đừng đổi giả định.
+**Owner decision on the A1/A4 conflict (2026-11-08), verbatim:**
+> Giữ Team và bỏ merge queue.
+So the design assumes **Team and no merge queue**. A4 is superseded. Its row below is kept only
+as a reference for a possible later move to Enterprise Cloud; the design does not use it.
**Consequences for the design.** These are my inferences from 3.1–3.6, unless a source is given.
The "cheap to cover the other case" lines do not change the assumptions.

| A1 — GitHub **Team** | Environment approval gates are unavailable on the private monorepo (3.1.2). **The approval gate is the PR merge to `main`, enforced by rulesets** (3.2.1–3.2.4): PR required, approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, approval after the last push, and an empty bypass list. The `production` environment is restricted to `main` (3.1.3). All the prerequisites in 3.6 #1 apply: only reviewed deploy workflows reference `production`, deploys take no ref input, and no privileged triggers are used. Admin edits are logged, not prevented. Drift detection is needed (3.1.4, 3.6 #1). | Create the `production` environment now, with the branch restriction. If Papaya moves to Enterprise Cloud, add required reviewers, prevent self-review, and disallow admin bypass on that environment. This is a settings change only; the workflows and the OIDC trust stay the same (inference). |

| A2 — immutable `sub` (with IDs) | AWS and GCP trust conditions must match `repo:<owner>@<owner-id>/<repo>@<repo-id>:environment:production` (inference from the documented `ref` examples), with placeholders in `examples/` (3.4.4). If the `sub` is customised with `job_workflow_ref` (3.4.5), the IDs stay in the `repo` segment and cannot be removed (3.4.4, oidc reference). | The org or repo can **opt in** to immutable subject claims (3.4.4). Opting in makes A2 true regardless of the repo's creation date. Accepting the old format as well would bring back the namespace-recycling risk, so it is not recommended. |

| A3 — worst case: the app is the PR author, and the person who triggered the agent can approve | The built-in "authors cannot approve" rule cannot be relied on (3.3.1, 3.3.4). Protected branches need **2 approvals**, at least on paths an agent can change, **or** a required status check whose **expected source app is pinned** (3.2.5, 3.3.4). content.content:
An update plan constrains the pulumi up operation to allow only the changes described in the plan. No other changes will be applied.
It's important to note that the plan is not evaluated in an all-or-nothing fashion before changes are applied. Instead, update operations run in batches as the program execution progresses and resources resolve their input values. At any point, if any discrepancy between the plan and the actual exec
This approach ensures that only planned changes are applied while allowing for the natural resolution of resource dependencies during execution.
## Limitations
Update plans can only record information that is available at preview time. This means there are some program
constructs that while possible to run correctly at update time, can't be recorded at preview time.
The most common one is inputs set by the output of other resources that are being created. While the plan will
record that the program wants to set the input field, it can't record the value which it will be set with and
simply records `unknown`.
The next most common issue is creating resources inside an [`apply`
function](/docs/iac/concepts/inputs-outputs/apply/). If the value for the apply is
unknown at preview time, then the apply function will not run. This results in the plan not recording
anything for the resources created inside the apply and reporting an error at update time when they try to
create. This mostly comes up in the context of needing to create a resource for every item in an array, we
have [an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/issues/4834) tracking support for this.
The final issue is configuring explicit providers with unknown inputs. Providers configured with unknowns
currently do not do full checks and diffs of resources at preview time, this can result in the plan not
including information about default, or normalized values which then get set during the actual update.
The first limitation should not prevent the use of plans, it simply makes them a little harder to review and
not as strong a guarantee as to what the program will do. We will be looking at improving the precision here.
The other two are best worked around today by splitting your stacks up and using stack references to pass the
values forward. Stack reference values are never unknown (because the other stack must have run by the time
they're used).
## Format

# AWS - Diff
The `sls diff` command shows the difference between the CloudFormation template generated from your current configuration and the stack currently deployed in AWS. It is useful for reviewing changes before running `sls deploy`, especially in CI / PR-review workflows.
```bash
serverless diff
```
Two orthogonal signals are surfaced:
1. **Function Code changes** — per-function comparison of the locally-packaged zip against each Lambda's `CodeSha256` in AWS. Tells you which functions will have their code redeployed. A service with [web apps](../guide/web-apps.md) also gets a **Web App Code** section, which lists the web apps whose code is new or changed against the deployed stack.
2. **CloudFormation template diff** — a structured diff of resources, IAM statements, security groups, parameters, outputs, and other top-level template sections. Tells you what CloudFormation will change.
By default, the service is packaged first so the local template reflects the current configuration on disk. If you already have a packaged artifact directory (for example, from a previous CI step), pass `--package <path>` to use it directly and skip repackaging.
## Options
- `--stage` or `-s` The service stage to diff against. Defaults to the stage from `serverless.yml` or `dev`.
- `--region` or `-r` The service region to diff against.
- `--aws-profile` The AWS profile to use.
- `--stack` CloudFormation stack name override.
- `--package` or `-p` Path to an existing package directory to diff against. Skips the auto-package step when set.
- `--json` Output the diff in JSON format. Suitable for CI consumption.
## Provided lifecycle events
- `diff:diff`

# Reconcile
The `reconcile` command reconciles your org's list of billable instances with the actual CloudFormation stacks currently in your AWS account, making it an essential tool to recover credits for stacks that were removed manually without running the `remove` command.
We generally recommend to always use the `remove` command to remove Serverless Framework stacks to ensure the removal is reported, but if you must remove stacks manually or your organization has a custom workflow, this command is the only way for us to know that your service instance was removed and that it should no longer be consuming credits.
**Note:** The `reconcile` command is a global, account-wide command. It is **not** a per-service command and does **not** need to be run from inside a service directory. A single invocation reconciles every billable instance reported for your org against all CloudFormation stacks in the AWS account associated with the credentials it is run with, so you only need to run it once per AWS account — 
If you have Serverless Framework stacks in multiple AWS accounts, you should run this command once for each AWS account (using credentials for that account) for a complete reconciliation and more accurate usage reporting and billing.
**Note:** This command might take a few minutes to complete depending on how many CloudFormation stacks you have in your AWS account.
### AWS Region Configuration
By default, the `reconcile` command uses the `us-east-1` region to fetch your AWS account ID. If you're working in a restricted environment where access to specific regions is blocked or where VPC endpoints are only available for certain regions, you can override this default behavior by setting the `AWS_REGION` environment variable:
```bash
AWS_REGION=eu-central-1 serverless reconcile
```
## Usage
```bash
serverless reconcile
```
The command can be run from **any directory** — it does not need to be executed inside a service directory and does not read your `serverless.yml`. It operates at the AWS account level using the AWS credentials available in your environment.
## Options
- `--org` The org name to reconcile instances for. Defaults to your service org if found, or your default personal org.
## Example
The example below runs `reconcile` from an arbitrary directory (no `serverless.yml` required):
```
~ $ serverless reconcile
Successfully recovered 3 Instance Credits from the 123456789012 AWS account.
If you have any questions about your usage, please contact support@serverless.com.
~ $

### How It Works
The Serverless Framework translates all syntax in `serverless.yml` to a single AWS CloudFormation template. By depending on CloudFormation for deployments, users of the Serverless Framework get the safety and reliability of CloudFormation.
- An AWS CloudFormation template is created from your `serverless.yml`.
- If a Stack has not yet been created, then it is created with no resources except for an S3 Bucket, which will store zip files of your Function code.
- If you're using locally build ECR images, dedicated ECR repository is created for your service. You also will be logged to that repository via `docker login` if needed.
- The code of your Functions is then packaged into zip files.
- If you're using locally build ECR images, they are built and uploaded to ECR.
- Serverless fetches the hashes for all files of the previous deployment (if any) and compares them against the hashes of the local files.
- Serverless terminates the deployment process if all file hashes are the same.
- Zip files of your Functions' code are uploaded to your Code S3 Bucket.
- Any IAM Roles, Functions, Events and Resources are added to the AWS CloudFormation template.
- The CloudFormation Stack is updated with the new CloudFormation template.
- Each deployment publishes a new version for each function in your service.
**Note:** AWS SSM and S3 permissions are required for deployments to manage state and upload deployment packages. For more details, see [AWS Credentials Requirement for Packaging](./packaging.md#aws-credentials-requirement-for-packaging).
### Deployment method
Since Serverless Framework v4, deployments are by default done using [CloudFormation direct deployments](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-direct.html). This is the recommended approach for most users.
If you want to instead use [CloudFormation change sets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-changesets.html), you can enable it via the `deploymentMethod` option:
```yml
provider:
  name: aws

### How It Works
The Serverless Framework translates all syntax in `serverless.yml` to a single AWS CloudFormation template. By depending on CloudFormation for deployments, users of the Serverless Framework get the safety and reliability of CloudFormation.
- An AWS CloudFormation template is created from your `serverless.yml`.
- If a Stack has not yet been created, then it is created with no resources except for an S3 Bucket, which will store zip files of your Function code.
- If you're using locally build ECR images, dedicated ECR repository is created for your service. You also will be logged to that repository via `docker login` if needed.
- The code of your Functions is then packaged into zip files.
- If you're using locally build ECR images, they are built and uploaded to ECR.
- Serverless fetches the hashes for all files of the previous deployment (if any) and compares them against the hashes of the local files.
- Serverless terminates the deployment process if all file hashes are the same.
- Zip files of your Functions' code are uploaded to your Code S3 Bucket.
- Any IAM Roles, Functions, Events and Resources are added to the AWS CloudFormation template.
- The CloudFormation Stack is updated with the new CloudFormation template.
- Each deployment publishes a new version for each function in your service.
**Note:** AWS SSM and S3 permissions are required for deployments to manage state and upload deployment packages. For more details, see [AWS Credentials Requirement for Packaging](./packaging.md#aws-credentials-requirement-for-packaging).
### Deployment method
Since Serverless Framework v4, deployments are by default done using [CloudFormation direct deployments](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-direct.html). This is the recommended approach for most users.
If you want to instead use [CloudFormation change sets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-changesets.html), you can enable it via the `deploymentMethod` option:
```yml
provider:
  name: aws
  deploymentMethod: changesets
```

# Serverless Framework State
Serverless Framework Compose allows for the orchestration and deployment of multiple services.
A crucial aspect of this is managing the state of each service, which includes storing outputs and other runtime information necessary for the correct operation of services.
This guide covers how to set up and manage state using AWS S3 and AWS SSM.
## State Management Overview
State management in Serverless Framework Compose is crucial for:
- **Storing Service Outputs**: Save outputs from deployments to share them across services.
- **Ensuring Consistency**: Maintain the state of services across deployments, ensuring that each service can access the necessary data for its operation.
- **Handling Dependencies**: Automatically resolve dependencies between services by referencing shared state.
Serverless Framework Compose uses AWS S3 to store the state of services and AWS SSM (Systems Manager) to track the location of the state storage.
## Zero-Configuration Setup
The easiest way to manage state in Serverless Framework Compose is through its default, zero-configuration setup. When you don’t specify any state configuration, Serverless Framework Compose automatically handles everything for you.
### How It Works
1. **Automatic S3 Bucket Creation**: If no state configuration is provided in your `serverless-compose.yml`, Serverless Framework Compose automatically creates an S3 bucket to store the state.
2. **SSM Parameter Store**: The name and region of the automatically created S3 bucket are stored in AWS SSM Parameter Store in `us-east-1` AWS region, under the parameter `/serverless-framework/state/s3-bucket`. This parameter contains a JSON object with the following keys:
- `bucketName`: The name of the S3 bucket.
- `bucketRegion`: The AWS region where the bucket is located.
3. **Versioning Enabled**: The created S3 bucket will have versioning enabled by default, ensuring that different states over time are maintained and can be rolled back if necessary.
**Note**: To create the default state bucket, you must have the necessary permissions to put SSM parameters and create versioned S3 buckets.
If you don’t have these permissions, you can set up a [custom state configuration](#custom-state-configuration) to use an existing S3 bucket.

# Serverless Framework License Keys
Starting with Version 4, authentication is required for all users of the Serverless Framework CLI, and License Keys are one method of providing this authentication.
## What Are License Keys And When You Need Them
License Keys are merely unique identifiers used to authenticate your access to Serverless Framework V4 and ensure compliance with its licensing model.
They're ideal for organizations that prefer not to use the Serverless Framework Dashboard or its authentication methods. If you want to use only the CLI and avoid remote requests to the Dashboard, License Keys are the solution.
Paid Users and Serverless Framework Dashboard users can optionally use License Keys, or can authenticate through the Dashboard. The CLI provides guidance for Dashboard authentication. Please note that you must have an active subscription to use License Keys.
- **Simple Identifiers**: License Keys in the Serverless Framework merely serve to validate and track subscription usage. They do not offer access control or permissions within the CLI or Dashboard.
- **Disables Dashboard Access**: License Keys will disable access to the Serverless Framework Dashboard. This eliminates all remote requests to the Dashboard, except for validating the License Key and sending License Key telemetry.
- **No Expiration**: License Keys do not have an expiration date. This provides consistent access to the Framework without the need to regularly update keys. However, you should still periodically rotate keys as a best practice.
- **Create One or Several**: Create and distribute as many License Keys as needed across your organization - whether by company, team, app, or developer.
## How to Manage License Keys
There are two ways to manage License Keys:
You can manually create, list and delete them within the Serverless Framework Dashboard within the [Settings > License Keys view](https://app.serverless.com/settings/licenseKeys).
Or, you can programatically create, list and delete License Keys using our public API. But first, you need to get your orgId from within the [Settings > General view](https://app.serverless.com/settings/general) and create an access key from within the [Settings > Access Keys view](https://app.serve

Drift detection enables you to detect whether a stack's actual configuration differs, or has *drifted*, from its expected configuration. You can specify an IAM role that allows CloudFormation to create, update, or delete your stack resources. By default, CloudFormation uses a temporary session that it generates from your user credentials for stack operations. If you specify a service Use a service role to explicitly specify the actions that CloudFormation can perform, which might not always be the same actions that you or other users can do. For example, you might have administrative privileges, but you can limit CloudFormation access to only Amazon EC2 actions. You create the service role and its permission policy with the IAM service. For more information about creating a service role, see [Create a role to delegate permissions to an AWS service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_create_for-service.html) in the *IAM User Guide*. Specify CloudFormation (`cloudformation.amazonaws.com`) as the service that can assume the role. To associate a service role with a stack, specify the role when you create the stack. For details, see [Configure stack options](cfn-console-create-stack.md#configure-stack-options).
